title: Test: Calculus into a first neural network

questions.question: On the first page, how is the car's speed found from nothing but its positions?

options.text: Divide the change in position by the time it took, then shrink the gap
options.why: Between two positions a small gap apart, a change divided by a change, with the gap made as small as wanted, is the derivative.

options.text: Divide the current position by the whole time since the start of the trip
options.why: That is the average speed over the whole trip. It misses how fast the car goes at one moment.

options.text: Take the distance between two nearby positions, without dividing by the time
options.why: Distance alone depends on the gap chosen. Dividing by the time taken turns it into a speed.

options.text: Add up the positions over time, as the area under the curve
options.why: Adding up is the integral, which goes the other way: from speed back to distance.

questions.question: The perceptron finds a separating line on two clouds of dots, but on exclusive or it never stops. Why?

options.text: Its step size is too large, so each correction overshoots the four dots
options.why: Changing the step size does not help. The answer needs a bent boundary, which one line cannot give.

options.text: Four dots are too few for the rule to learn a boundary from
options.why: The number of dots is not the issue. A network with a middle layer learns the same four dots.

options.text: No straight line puts all four dots on their own sides
options.why: So there is always a dot left to correct. The rule can only turn and shift one line, and when no line works, every correction leaves a wrong dot.

options.text: It corrects every dot at once instead of one dot at a time
options.why: The perceptron does look at one dot at a time. It fails because no single line exists.

questions.question: On the landscape page, what does the gradient arrow under the ball show, and which way does the ball step?

options.text: The steepest way downhill; the ball steps along the arrow
options.why: The gradient points uphill. Descent goes against it, which is why the step has a minus sign.

options.text: The steepest way uphill; the ball steps the opposite way
options.why: The arrow's length gives how steep the ground is. Gradient descent subtracts the step size times the gradient, so each step goes against the uphill arrow.

options.text: The direction from the ball to the lowest point of the whole landscape
options.why: The ball knows only the ground under its feet. The gradient is local and can point away from the true bottom.

options.text: The way uphill, and the ball steps along it to climb
options.why: Following the arrow climbs. The goal is the bottom, so the step goes the other way.

questions.question: A car's position is s = 0.4t² metres. At t = 4 s it is at 6.4 m and at t = 6 s at 14.4 m. What speed does the two-position rule give at t = 5 s?

options.why: 8.0 m is the distance moved. It has to be divided by the 2 seconds it took.
That is s(5) / 5 = 10 / 5, the average speed since the start, not the speed at t = 5.

options.text: About 3.9 m/s, since a wide gap always undershoots
options.why: For a car with constant acceleration the two-position rule has no error at all. The true speed, 0.8 × 5 = 4.0, comes out exactly.

options.text: 4.0 m/s, exactly the true speed
options.why: (14.4 - 6.4) / 2 = 4.0. The rule's error depends on the third derivative, which is zero for 0.4t², so even a wide gap is exact.

questions.question: An amount grows by 7 per cent of itself each year, dA/dt = 0.07A. About how long does each doubling take?

options.text: About 14.3 years, 1 / 0.07
options.why: That is the doubling time for growth by a fixed amount each year. Growth by a fixed fraction of itself is faster.

options.text: About 9.9 years, ln 2 / 0.07
options.why: The exponential doubles every ln 2 / r. With r = 0.07 this is 9.9 years, and it is the same for every doubling.

options.text: It depends on the starting amount
options.why: Every doubling takes the same time, whatever the start, which is why the doubling ticks on the page are evenly spaced.

options.text: About 0.1 years
options.why: This divides the rate by ln 2 instead of ln 2 by the rate. A small rate means a long doubling time, not a short one.

questions.question: A perceptron has w = (1, -1), b = 0 and step size 0.5. The dot (1, 2) belongs on the 1 side. What does one correction do?

options.text: w becomes (1.5, 0) and b becomes 0.5
options.why: The total is 1 - 2 + 0 = -1, so the unit answers 0 and the dot is wrong. The rule adds 0.5 × (1 - 0) × (1, 2) to w and 0.5 to b; the new total, 2, is on the right side.

options.text: Nothing changes, because the dot is already on the right side
options.why: The total is -1, which is not above zero, so the unit answers 0 and the dot needs a correction.

options.text: w becomes (0.5, -2) and b becomes -0.5
options.why: This subtracts the correction. The rule turns the line towards a wrong dot, using y minus the answer, which is +1 here.

options.text: w becomes (1.5, 0) and b stays 0
options.why: The bias is corrected too, by the step size times the miss. Without that the line could only turn about the origin.

questions.question: A picture of 28 by 28 pixels is scanned by a 5 by 5 pattern at every position, then each 2 by 2 block keeps only its largest value. How many numbers are left?

options.text: 784 in the map, one per pixel, then 196
options.why: This assumes the pattern fits at every pixel. A 5 by 5 pattern must lie wholly inside the picture, so each side loses 4 positions.

options.text: 529 in the map, then 121
options.why: This counts 28 - 5 = 23 positions. Both the first and the last position count, so it is 28 - 5 + 1 = 24.

options.text: 576 in the map, then 288
options.why: Pooling keeps one number from each block of four, so the count falls by four, not by two.

options.text: 576 in the map, then 144
options.why: The pattern fits at 28 - 5 + 1 = 24 positions each way, so 24 × 24 = 576. Pooling halves each side, leaving 12 × 12 = 144.

questions.question: Why does training by descent need a smooth squash instead of the perceptron's hard yes-or-no?

options.text: The smooth squash is faster to compute than the hard threshold
options.why: The hard threshold is cheaper. Speed is not the reason; having a slope is.

options.text: The hard unit can only draw curves, never the straight line a boundary needs
options.why: It is the other way round: the hard unit draws exactly a straight line. The smooth unit draws the same line where it answers one half.

options.text: The smooth answer has a slope to follow; the hard answer is flat, then jumps
options.why: The smooth answer changes a little with each small nudge, so its slope shows which way to move. The move on a weight is the squash's slope times the input; for a hard step that slope is zero everywhere except at the jump, where it is not a number.

options.text: A smooth squash always gives the right answer, so training has no misses to correct
options.why: A smooth unit can be wrong, and starts wrong. Its mistakes come with a direction to fix them, which is the point.

questions.question: A unit with one input of 1 starts by answering 0.9 when the right answer is 0. Why does it correct slowly under the squared miss but not under cross entropy?

options.text: The squared miss scales the move by the squash's slope, small on the flat; cross entropy cancels it
options.why: Cross entropy leaves the miss itself. At an answer of 0.9 the slope is 0.9 × 0.1 = 0.09, so the squared miss moves w by 0.9 × 0.09 = 0.081, against 0.9 under cross entropy.

options.text: Cross entropy uses a larger step size, so each of its moves is longer
options.why: Both copies use the same step size. The difference is in the move each cost asks for.

options.text: The squared miss points the wrong way for a yes-or-no answer and has to turn back
options.why: It points the right way; it is only slow. The page calls it not wrong, but slow in the case that matters most.

options.text: A sure answer sits where the squash's slope is large, so the squared miss overshoots on every step
options.why: A sure answer sits on the flat part of the squash, where the slope is near zero. The move is too small, not too big.

questions.question: A deep network of squashes to 0..1, with small weights, sends blame back through five layers. Why does the first layer learn last?

options.text: The first layer is updated last in each step, so it has to wait until all the later layers have moved
options.why: All layers move in the same step, from one pass back. The first layer moves least because its blame is the smallest.

options.text: Each layer back multiplies the blame by at most 1/4, so after five it is at least 4^5 = 1024 times smaller
options.why: The largest slope of the squash is 1/4, and the factors multiply. The first layer, the one that sees the dots, receives the faintest blame and barely moves.

options.text: The first layer has fewer weights than the others, so it has less to learn with
options.why: Every hidden layer on the page has six units. The shortfall comes from the multiplying factors, not from a count of weights.

options.text: Each layer back adds 1/4 to the blame, so after five layers it is too large to use
options.why: The factors multiply rather than add, and each is below one, so the blame fades instead of growing.
